clinicalPearls: An autosomal dominant haemolytic anaemia caused most often by gain-of-function mutations in PIEZO1 (a mechanosensitive cation channel), and less commonly in KCNN4 (the Gardos channel)
Red cells are dehydrated with a high mean corpuscular haemoglobin concentration and often only mild anaemia with reticulocytosis
The blood film may show occasional stomatocytes and target cells, but changes can be subtle
Perinatal oedema or transient hydrops fetalis is a recognised association with PIEZO1 mutations
Iron overload is common and may occur out of proportion to transfusion, so ferritin should be monitored
Splenectomy is contraindicated because it markedly increases the risk of venous and thrombotic complications without reliably correcting the anaemia
Osmotic fragility is characteristically decreased (the cells are dehydrated and resist osmotic lysis), the opposite of hereditary spherocytosis
Diagnosis integrates red-cell indices, ektacytometry (osmotic gradient) findings, and genetic testing of PIEZO1 and KCNN4
reference.pathophysiology: In hereditary xerocytosis, gain-of-function mutations in the mechanosensitive channel PIEZO1 cause delayed channel inactivation and excessive cation leak, while KCNN4 (Gardos channel) mutations enhance calcium-activated potassium efflux. Both lead to net loss of intracellular potassium and water, dehydrating the red cell and raising its haemoglobin concentration. The rigid, dehydrated cells are prematurely removed, producing a compensated or mild haemolytic anaemia; the accompanying dysregulation of iron handling contributes to iron loading, and splenectomy is hazardous because the residual abnormal cells promote thrombosis.
additionalDifferentials: Acquired stomatocytosis (for example alcohol-related liver disease)
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and reticulocyte count with attention to a raised mean corpuscular haemoglobin concentration
Peripheral blood film for stomatocytes and target cells
Osmotic gradient ektacytometry showing the characteristic dehydrated red-cell curve
Genetic testing for PIEZO1 and KCNN4 mutations
Iron studies including ferritin to detect overload
Haemolysis markers and exclusion of membrane and enzyme disorders
redFlags: Fetal or neonatal oedema/hydrops in an affected pregnancy
Thrombotic or venous complications, particularly if splenectomy has been performed
Progressive iron overload with organ dysfunction
Severe or decompensated anaemia during intercurrent illness
reference.prognosis: Anaemia is usually mild or compensated with a good life expectancy, but iron overload and, in those who have undergone splenectomy, thromboembolic disease are the principal long-term risks.
pitfalls: Performing splenectomy for presumed haemolytic anaemia, which raises thrombotic risk without benefit
Misdiagnosing the condition as hereditary spherocytosis despite the opposite (decreased) osmotic fragility
Ignoring iron overload because the patient is not transfusion dependent
Overlooking the diagnosis when film changes are subtle and indices near normal
references: Nathan and Oski's Hematology and Oncology of Infancy and Childhood
